6Use it well

Brief clearly, manage context, verify.

ⓘ Notes
With the same agent, results swing on how clearly you brief it and how clean the context is: say the four things, give what is relevant, plan, verify, keep safe habits.

Why it’s designed this way: The model only sees what you give it; these habits all help it see the right things.

② Diagram

🧒 In plain words first

The helper only sees what you give it; it cannot guess what you meant but did not say. Like asking someone to shop for you: “get some food” versus “what to buy, who it is for, the budget, and when to deliver” gives very different results.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

The model sees only what you give it, never the requirements you kept in your head. So the key is on your side:

  • A clear task brief: state all four: goal, background, constraints, acceptance.
  • Managing context: give what is relevant, remove what is not.
  • Plan before acting, verify results yourself, keep safe habits.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

When giving a task, make four things clear: the result you want, the background, what must not be touched, and what counts as done. Adding one example often helps more than extra paragraphs. For complex jobs, have it write a plan first and check it before it starts.

Go deeper (the full explanation)
SayMeaning
🎯 GoalThe result you want (not “make it better”)
📎 BackgroundWhere the material is, who it is for, what was tried
🚫 ConstraintsWhat must not be touched or done
✅ AcceptanceWhat counts as done, and how it can check

❌ “Make my report a bit better.”

✅ “Turn docs/q3-report.md into a one-page summary for management (goal). Readers have no time for detail; they care about cost and risk (background). Do not change any numbers (constraint). Done means: under 250 words, and the first three sentences state the conclusion (acceptance).”

One more trick: an example often works better than three more paragraphs of rules. For complex tasks, have it write a plan and approve it before it acts, matching the “think first” in ③ Think / decide (LLM).

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

The helper’s “desk” (its context) is limited in size, and the fuller it gets, the easier it is for important things to get buried. So: one topic per chat; tell it where a file is rather than pasting the whole thing; and take away material unrelated to the task.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

To be more exact…Research found that many models make worse use of information in the middle of a long text than at its start or end; this is a general tendency that varies between models.

At each step the model sees only what is in the Context window, counted in tokens cut by the Tokenizer. The window has a limit, and the more it holds, the easier key facts get buried: studies found many models use information in the middle of a long context less well than at the start or end. It is a common tendency, stronger in some models than others.

  • One topic per chat: new topic, new chat; when a chat runs long, have it write a summary and carry that over.
  • Give paths, not whole files: tell the agent where files are and let it read what it needs.
  • Remove irrelevant material: extra documents do not just waste room, they can lead it astray.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

“Done” from the helper does not mean really done. First have it check its own work (run tests, compare with the requirements), then spot-check the important parts yourself: numbers, quotes, dates and anything to be sent out. Look at the evidence, not just what it says.

Go deeper (the full explanation)
  • Have it check first: ask it to run tests, go through the acceptance criteria one by one, and say where it is unsure.
  • Then spot-check the key parts: numbers, sources, dates, anything going out.
  • “It says done” is not done: models can be confidently wrong; look at evidence (test results, diffs, original sources).
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

A few good habits: start with few keys and take them back afterwards; always approve sending, deleting and paying yourself; web pages and emails it reads may hide bad instructions; and never paste passwords into the chat.

Go deeper (the full explanation)
  • Start with little access, just enough; take it back when the task is done.
  • Keep human confirmation for irreversible actions: sending, deleting, paying.
  • Web pages, emails and files it reads may hide a Prompt injection; an agent that reads outside content should not also hold send and delete rights.
  • Never paste passwords or keys into the chat.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

What comes back is like homework handed in, to be marked against a checklist: for code, check the tests really passed; for reports, open a few sources; for tables, check the totals; for anything to be sent, check the recipients. If it fails, send it back and say which item failed.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

Write the acceptance criteria when you hand the task off, not after you see the result. Common checks by type of output:

OutputCheck at least
Code / PRTests really ran and passed (read the log, not just its word); read the diff for files outside the task; check it didn’t delete tests or skip checks to “pass”.
Report / researchOpen a few citations and compare with the source; are sources primary and authoritative; did it skip any question you asked; are dates and numbers right.
Data / tablesRow counts and totals match the source; pick a few random rows and trace them back; how blanks and outliers were handled.
Anything going outRight recipients, names and attachments; nothing that shouldn’t leave; you press “send” yourself.
  • You looked at every place it said it was unsure about.
  • The result reproduces: a rerun, or you following the steps, gives the same conclusion.
  • If it fails, send it back saying which item failed, rather than quietly fixing it yourself.

For reference: one AI lab, evaluating its research agents, scored factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality and tool efficiency.

Sources: How we built our multi-agent research system

🧪 The four switches: the clearer the brief, the better

🧒 In plain words first

Switch on the four parts of “making it clear” one by one and watch the score change; then add some unrelated documents and see whether the score drops (the score is an illustrative teaching score).

ⓘ The “expected quality” score is an illustrative teaching score, not a measurement of a real model.

Why it’s built this way:
  • Split “say it clearly” into four switches and turn them on one by one to see which matters most.
  • Extra irrelevant documents cost points: more context is not always better.

Original request: “Make my report a bit better.”
